doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Learning from mistakes; Miles Davis as a true artist
summary: He learned teaching from his mistakes and admires Miles Davis's constant change.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Right. And that’s the thing, to learn how to recover and to react to your mistakes and that’s how we learn. We don’t learn from doing the same things over and over again. I’ve learned more from the mistakes I’ve made that has helped me to become a better teacher. Because I know what you’re going through and I know what you’re doing because I’ve done that so I can tell you what you need to do to kind of correct that or whatever. But it’s beautiful. I think Miles Davis’ style was more out of his weaknesses than his strengths as he developed. I mean in the beginning he would sound like Dizzy Gillespie and when he was hanging around with Charlie Parker and those guys. But sooner or later Miles started developing into these things and then from the forties, fifties, sixties, seventies, eighties, up until the nineties Miles was changing man. He didn’t stay the same.
I know. Just seems like when you got into what he was doing he was on to something else.

He was a true artist man. I think he was really a true artist. Not only with music but fashion and visual art. Yeah he was what I call a true artist. And a lot of people didn’t like what he was doing toward the end but I loved it and I love it man, I love Miles.
